title: Commas
note: Use a comma before and, but, or, nor, for, so or yet when it joins two independent clauses; after most introductory elements; around nonessential information; between items in a series and between coordinate adjectives; and in dates and addresses. Never put a single comma between a subject and its verb.

src.t: Purdue OWL, Extended Rules for Using Commas

items.a: I ran, but I missed the bus.
d: I ran but, I missed the bus.
I ran, but, I missed the bus.

items.ex: No comma between two verbs that share one subject.

items.a: While we ate, the dog begged.
d: While we ate the dog begged.
items.ex: Without the comma, readers first think we ate the dog.

items.a: My mother, who lives in Erie, called.
d: My mother who lives in Erie called.
My mother, who lives in Erie called.

items.ex: With commas, the sentence says all students cheat.

items.a: The man in the gray coat left.
d: The man in the gray coat, left.

items.a: Erie, Pennsylvania, is on a lake.

Erie Pennsylvania, is on a lake.

items.a: information you can remove without changing the core meaning

read.title: Commas that change meaning
text: Many comma rules exist for one reason: to stop the reader from grouping words the wrong way. "While we ate the dog begged" invites a horrifying first reading. A comma after ate fixes it at once.

The most important comma decision involves essential and nonessential information. Compare two sentences. "My cousin who lives in Ohio is a nurse" has no commas, which tells the reader the clause is essential: you have several cousins, and this one is identified by living in Ohio. "My cousin, who lives in Ohio, is a nurse" sets the clause off, which tells the reader it is extra: you have one cousin, and by the way, she lives in Ohio. The words are the same; the commas change the facts.

Commas also mark the seam between two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction: "The store opened, and the line began to move." But a comma never comes between a subject and its verb, however long the subject grows. "The store on the corner of Fifth and Main opened" needs no comma at all.

q.q: What does "My cousin, who lives in Ohio, is a nurse" suggest?
o: The cousin is not a nurse

q.q: Why does "While we ate the dog begged" need a comma?
o: To prevent a wrong first reading
To separate a subject from its verb

q.q: According to the reading, where does a comma never go?
o: Between a subject and its verb
